Empirical Research Plan: 1970 CAA Non-attainment Designations, TSP, and Housing Prices  

------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
------------------------------------------------------------  
Method: Two–stage least squares difference-in-differences (2SLS-DiD).

•  First stage (DiD): estimate the causal effect of being classified “non-attainment” on county-level TSP concentrations.  
•  Second stage (IV): use the predicted (exogenous) component of TSP to estimate its impact on log median owner-occupied housing value.

Why this strategy?  
a) The Clean Air Act generated a discrete, plausibly exogenous compliance shock that varied across counties and time (1972 onward).  
b) We care about the causal effect of a continuous endogenous regressor (pollution) on prices; non-attainment is a powerful instrument but not of direct economic interest because it also changes regulation costs.  
c) A panel IV with two-way fixed effects absorbs unobserved county fundamentals and nationwide time shocks, satisfying a DiD structure while solving the simultaneity/measurement-error problem in pollution.

------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
------------------------------------------------------------  
Treatment variable (instrument):  
  Z_it = NonAttain_i × Post_t   
 NonAttain_i = 1 if county i was designated non-attainment for TSP in the initial 1972 list (or 0 otherwise).  
 Post_t = 1 for t ≥ 1972 (or use 1972–1976 for the 1970 CAA regime and allow a second shock in 1978 for the 1977 Amendments in robustness).

Control group: counties that were in attainment status in 1972 (Z_it = 0 through 1976). These counties faced only light monitoring and minimal federal oversight.

Treatment timing: January 1972 is the implementation date of initial non-attainment designations; enforcement intensifies again in 1978. Baseline pre-period is 1968–1971 (only 1971 observed in AQS); post-period 1972–1990.

Running variable / cutoff: not applicable (this is not an RDD design).

Dependent variable (main outcome): ln(Value_it) = natural log of median owner-occupied housing value in county i, year t.

Endogenous regressor: TSP_it (μg/m³ annual geometric mean).

------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
------------------------------------------------------------  
A1. Relevance (first-stage): Non-attainment status must significantly reduce TSP.  
 Plausibility: EPA compliance data and engineering studies document 10-25% TSP declines in non-attainment counties relative to attainment by mid-1970s.

A2. Exogeneity/parallel trends: In the absence of designation, housing values in future non-attainment and attainment counties would have followed parallel paths.  
 Plausibility: Designation was an administrative rule based primarily on 1971 monitor data relative to the 75 µg/m³ standard, a variable we can control for and interact with trends.

A3. Exclusion restriction: Non-attainment affects housing prices only through its impact on air quality, not via other channels (e.g., slower industrial growth).  
 Plausibility: Potentially violated; we will control for contemporaneous employment, income, and housing supply to mitigate. We also interpret our estimates as “local average WTP for cleaner air net of any regulatory-cost capitalization.”

A4. Stable unit treatment value (no spatial spillovers): TSP abatement in non-attainment counties does not directly change housing values in attainment neighbors.  
 Plausibility: Some downwind spillovers are possible; border-pair robustness checks will be conducted.

A5. No differential migration/compositional changes that themselves raise house prices independent of air quality.  
 Plausibility: Monitor with Census-based population inflow/outflow and include county-by-decade linear trends.

------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  
------------------------------------------------------------  
T1. Simultaneous local economic shocks (e.g., factory closures due to compliance costs) that influence prices.  
 Mitigation: Control for county-year employment, manufacturing payroll, unemployment, and property tax millage. Also run “business-cycle adjusted” specifications using state-year × industry employment shares.

T2. Sorting and demographic composition changes.  
 Mitigation: Include population, share college, racial composition, median income, and estimate bounds excluding the ten fastest-growing and ten fastest-shrinking counties. Check pre-trends in demographic variables.

T3. Measurement error in TSP or monitor siting manipulation.  
 Mitigation: Instrument deals with classical error; we also show robustness to alternative pollution metrics (90th percentile, 2nd-max 24-hour reading), drop counties with only one monitor, and restrict to counties with monitor continuity both before and after 1972.

------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline  
------------------------------------------------------------  
```r
#----------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
#----------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast load / merge
library(fixest)       # TWFE and IV estimation
library(did)          # event-study check
library(modelsummary) # tables

#----------------------------------------------
# 1. Load Data
#----------------------------------------------
cnty    <- fread("county_controls.csv")      # pop, income, etc.
price   <- fread("county_housing.csv")       # median value, 1970 $s
tsp     <- fread("county_tsp.csv")           # annual geom mean, μg/m³
attain  <- fread("nonattainment_status.csv") # 1 = non-attain, 0 = attain

# Merge
dt <- Reduce(function(x,y) merge(x,y, by = c("fips","year"), all = TRUE),
             list(cnty, price, tsp, attain))

#----------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable Construction
#----------------------------------------------
dt[, post      := (year >= 1972)]
dt[, nonatt72  := first(nonattain[year==1972]), by = fips]      # baseline status
dt[, Z         := nonatt72 * post]                              # instrument
dt[, ln_value  := log(median_value)]
dt[, year_fe   := factor(year)]
dt[, stateyear := interaction(state, year)]                     # state-year FE (robustness)

#----------------------------------------------
# 3. Main 2SLS-DiD Specification
#----------------------------------------------
# First-stage: effect of non-attainment on TSP
fs <- feols(tsp ~ Z | fips + year, data = dt)
summary(fs)

# Second-stage: WTP for cleaner air
iv <- feols(ln_value ~ 1 | fips + year | tsp ~ Z, data = dt,
            cluster = ~fips)
etable(fs, iv, se = "cluster")

#----------------------------------------------
# 4. Event-study Pre-trend Check
#----------------------------------------------
es <- att_gt(yname = "ln_value",
             gname = "first(nonattain[year==1972])",
             tname = "year",
             idname = "fips",
             data = dt[year<=1978])   # focus on early years
aggte_es <- aggte(es, type = "dynamic")
summary(aggte_es)
ggdid(aggte_es)

#----------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: Border-county Pair Fixed Effects
#----------------------------------------------
border <- fread("county_borders.csv")       # pairs of adjacent counties
dt2 <- merge(dt, border, by = "fips")
iv_border <- feols(ln_value ~ 1 | pair_id + year | tsp ~ Z,
                   data = dt2, cluster = ~pair_id)
summary(iv_border)
```

------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  
------------------------------------------------------------  
Theory yields a positive capitalisation of cleaner air: housing prices should rise when TSP falls. Prior empirical benchmarks (e.g., $100–$150 per μg/m³ in 1980 dollars) suggest:

• First stage: Non-attainment reduces TSP by roughly 6–10 μg/m³ (≈8–12 %).  
• Second stage: A 1 μg/m³ decline increases log median values by 0.05–0.10 %, implying WTP of about $1,000–$2,000 per household for a permanent 10 μg/m³ reduction (discounting at 5 %). The sign is therefore expected to be negative on TSP, positive on air quality.

------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DiD/IV)  
------------------------------------------------------------  
C1. Strong first-stage relevance …… 1  
C2. Parallel pre-treatment trends … 0.8 (looks good in event study)  
C3. Exclusion (no other channels)… 0.5 (possible industrial shocks)  
C4. No spillovers/interference …… 0.7  
C5. No sample composition changes… 0.6  

Overall: reasonably credible but requires robustness analyses to shore up C3–C5.
